passages.t: Four men at the gate, and an empty camp
passages.happening:
Elisha speaks the word of the LORD: about this time tomorrow, at the gate of Samaria, ‘a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel, and two seahs of barley will sell for a shekel’ (verse 1). The officer on whose arm the king leans answers, “Look, even if the LORD were to make windows in heaven, could this really happen?” (verse 2). “You will see it with your own eyes,” Elisha replies, “but you will not eat any of it” (verse 2).

Four men with leprosy sit at the entrance of the city gate. “Why just sit here until we die?” they say to one another (verse 3). If they go into the city they will die of famine, and if they stay they will die anyway. So at twilight they go over to the Aramean camp, and there is no one there (verses 4-5).

‘For the Lord had caused the Arameans to hear the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army’ (verse 6). They thought the king of Israel had hired the kings of the Hittites and of Egypt against them, and they fled at twilight, leaving their tents, horses and donkeys, running for their lives (verses 6-7). The four men go into a tent, eat and drink, and carry off silver, gold and clothing to hide. Then they go into another tent and do the same (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 6 ended at the lowest point of the siege, with the king vowing to kill Elisha and saying there was no use waiting for the LORD. This chapter is the LORD's answer, in two parts: a word, and its fulfillment down to the price of grain.

A seah was a dry measure of several liters, and a shekel a weight of silver of about eleven or twelve grams. A seah of fine flour for a shekel was an ordinary price, astonishing only beside the famine prices of 6:25. The officer was a senior royal aide. His mockery uses the picture of the windows of heaven opening to send rain or plenty. He means that nothing short of a miracle could change prices so fast, and he is right, though not as he meant.

Under the law, people with serious skin disease had to live outside the city, which is why the four men are at the gate. They lived on what people brought them, and in a siege no one brought anything. Their reasoning is that of people with nothing left to lose.

In the ninth century BC the Hittites meant the kingdoms of northern Syria and southeastern Turkey, such as Carchemish and Hamath, not the old Hittite empire, which had fallen centuries before. A threat from north and south at once would have made the Aramean position untenable. God never appears on stage. The narrator says only once what he did. The sound, qol, was enough; no army was there.
passages.later: The law said of a person with such a disease, ‘He must live alone in a place outside the camp’ (Leviticus 13:46). Malachi used the same picture as the officer: ‘See if I will not open the windows of heaven’ (Malachi 3:10).
passages.asks: God delivered the city by a sound in the enemy's ears, and the first to find out were four outcasts. Ask whether you have doubted what God can do because you could not see how he would do it. And ask whom you are inclined to overlook, who might be carrying news you need to hear.

passages.happening:
Then the four men stop. ‘We are not doing what is right. Today is a day of good news. If we are silent and wait until morning light, our sin will overtake us’ (verse 9). They go and call to the gatekeepers that the Aramean camp is empty, with only tethered horses and donkeys and the tents left standing (verse 10). The news is shouted into the king's household (verse 11).

The king gets up in the night and suspects a trap: the Arameans know the city is starving, he says, and are hiding in the field to catch the people when they come out (verse 12). One of his servants suggests sending scouts with some of the horses that are left, since those horses will die anyway (verse 13). The scouts follow the Arameans as far as the Jordan, and the whole road is littered with the clothing and equipment the Arameans threw away in their haste (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The four men's confession is the turning point of the chapter. Good news for a whole city cannot be kept for themselves. The word, besorah, is used for news of victory and, in Isaiah, for the announcement that God reigns and has come to save his people. The Greek translation of the Old Testament uses the word family from which the New Testament's word for gospel comes.

The king's suspicion adds a last moment of doubt, and it is an unnamed servant's practical suggestion that finally opens the city to its rescue. The road to the Jordan shows the Arameans heading east, toward Gilead and home to Damascus.
passages.later: Isaiah wrote, ‘How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news’ (Isaiah 52:7).
passages.asks: The four men knew that silence would be wrong. Ask what good news you have received that people around you are still waiting to hear. And ask whether, like the king, you have treated good news as a trap because you had stopped expecting any.

passages.t: Flour for a shekel, and the officer in the gate
passages.happening:
The people go out and plunder the Aramean camp, and ‘a seah of fine flour sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley sold for a shekel, according to the word of the LORD’ (verse 16).

The king had put the officer on whose arm he leaned in charge of the gate, ‘but the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died, just as the man of God had foretold’ (verse 17). The narrator repeats Elisha's word, the officer's mockery and Elisha's answer (verses 18-19), and ends, ‘And that is just what happened to him’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is built as prophecy, reversal and exact fulfillment. Elisha's word about prices is given in verse 1, repeated as fulfilled in verse 16, and recalled again in verse 18. The officer's mockery is quoted twice, and his death is told twice. The repetition drives home that every detail came true.

The city gate was the center of public life in ancient Israel: trade, law and news. It is fitting that the market reopens there, and that the officer appointed to keep order there dies there. His unbelief did not stop God's promise. It only shut him out of it. He saw the plenty with his own eyes and did not eat.
passages.later: Balaam, hired to curse Israel, had to say of the LORD, ‘Does He speak and not act? Does He promise and not fulfill?’ (Numbers 23:19).
passages.hard:
Is the officer's death a punishment for one sentence of doubt?

The text ties his death to Elisha's word and tells it plainly, twice. It does not say that God struck him. The people trampled him in the gateway. The chapter's concern is that the word of the LORD came true in every detail, including the warning to the man who mocked it. He was not a starving person afraid to hope. He was the king's chief aide, standing beside the king at the moment the LORD promised rescue, and he dismissed it out of hand.

It is not a lesson that doubt is punished with death, and it gives no one a reason to see an accident as a judgment.

A word of care. This story must not be used to say that a sudden death, an accident or an illness today is God's punishment on the person who suffered it. Jesus refused that kind of reasoning: of people killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). If you have lost someone suddenly, or carry fear or guilt after reading this, please speak with someone you trust, a pastor or a friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The officer saw the plenty and never tasted it. Ask how a person can stand close to what God is doing and still miss it. And ask whether there is a promise of God you have dismissed because you could not imagine how it would come true.
